name: O'Connell Monument
historical_description: Bronze monument to Daniel O'Connell, conceived by John Henry Foley in 1866 and completed by Thomas Brock in 1883. It includes a high-relief frieze and multiple figures around a granite plinth.

name: Central Hall, 71 Clontarf Road — 1906 Methodist hall
historical_description: Attached Methodist hall built in 1906, with a gabled south façade and a link block connecting it to the associated church. NIAH records a natural-slate roof, cast-iron rainwater goods, cut-granite verge stones and carved kneelers, crenellated parapet, rusticated granite walls and plinth, stained-glass pointed-arch windows, granite door surrounds, steps and threshold. The front elevation carries an inscribed sandstone plaque reading “Central Hall 1906”.
historical_significance: A documented early twentieth-century Methodist hall associated with an earlier church on the site (1867, extended 1881). NIAH attributes the 1906 hall to the builders Collen Brothers and the designs of W.M. Mitchell and Sons. The building preserves a legible date inscription and crafted granite and stained-glass details.
access_status: Hall and adjoining church have managed/private access. Photograph exterior from public footpath where visible; obtain permission before entering grounds or photographing interiors. Do not obstruct the footpath.

name: Clontarf Castle gate lodge — Gothic Revival entrance building
address: Entrance to Clontarf Castle, Castle Avenue, Clontarf, Dublin 3
historical_description: Detached complex-plan gate lodge built in 1836–37, comprising a three-bay, two-storey building with a three-stage round tower, gabled bay containing a former carriage arch, carved limestone spire and crenellated elements. NIAH records carved limestone coping, stringcourses, corbel table with sculpted animal heads, stepped buttresses, shield over the former carriage arch, pointed-arch openings, carved hood-mouldings, cut-limestone mullions and granite bollards linked by steel chains.
historical_significance: A richly detailed Gothic Revival gate lodge associated with Clontarf Castle. NIAH attributes the rebuilding to designs by William Vitruvius Morrison and notes that early Ordnance Survey maps show the avenue passing through the Tudor arch. The sculpted animal heads and carved limestone details are evidence of nineteenth-century stonemasonry.
access_status: At the entrance to Clontarf Castle Hotel, beside a road roundabout and private hotel grounds. Photograph only from a lawful, safe public viewpoint; do not enter hotel grounds or stand on the carriageway/roundabout without permission.

name: Clontarf Castle — Gothic Revival country house, rebuilt 1836–37
address: Clontarf Castle Hotel, Castle Avenue, Clontarf, Dublin 3
historical_description: Detached country house rebuilt in 1836–37, comprising a square-plan tower-house form with curved corners and a taller rear tower, attached to a complex-plan Gothic Revival house with gabled bays, porch and canted bay windows. NIAH records carved limestone copings and finials, crenellated parapets, octagonal chimneystacks, carved door surrounds and extensive surviving interior features including plasterwork ceilings, timber wainscoting and joinery, fireplaces and encaustic tiled floors. The building is now in use as a hotel.
historical_significance: The present castle is the 1836–37 Gothic Revival rebuilding commissioned by J.E.V. Vernon and designed by William Vitruvius Morrison. It deliberately uses medieval architectural references and varied tower forms to evoke a building developed over centuries. The NIAH appraisal identifies its carved stonework and surviving interior craftsmanship as significant.
access_status: The castle operates as a hotel. Photograph exterior only from lawful public viewpoints unless the hotel grants permission. Interior photography requires explicit venue permission; do not enter restricted areas.

name: Warrenpoint gate lodge — 84 Clontarf Road
historical_description: Detached two-bay single-storey former gate lodge, built circa 1840, with an entrance loggia on the east-facing front. NIAH records a hipped natural slate roof, red-brick chimneystacks with cornices and clay pots, carved fascia boards with cusping, cast-iron rainwater goods, lined-and-ruled rendered walls, label-moulded window openings and paired three-pane round-headed timber casements. The entrance is set within a group of red-brick gate piers, a segmental arch and masonry sphinx finials, with smooth rendered quadrant walls.
historical_significance: NIAH identifies this as one of the earliest buildings to develop on the Clontarf seafront, predating the associated terrace of six houses to the north-east. It is a rare surviving example of a nineteenth-century seafront gate lodge, retaining decorative roof, window and chimney details.
access_status: NIAH records the building as a private house. Photograph only from lawful public viewpoints; do not enter the property, shared grounds or private terrace. Confirm safe pedestrian access before photographing the gate piers and sphinx finials.

name: 86 Clontarf Road
historical_description: Terraced two-bay, two-storey house over a raised basement, built in 1847, with a two-storey return to the rear. NIAH records a pitched M-profile natural slate roof, front parapet with cut-granite platband and cornice, smooth-rendered chimneystacks, Flemish-bond brown-brick front elevation, granite stringcourse and rendered basement. The round-headed entrance has a petal-motif fanlight, a corniced and friezed door surround supported by console brackets, and a timber-panelled door. Cut-granite entrance steps and platform retain a cast-iron balustrade; the property is set back behind cast-iron railings on a cut-granite plinth and a pedestrian gate. A two-bay single-storey outbuilding survives to the rear, with later extensions.
historical_significance: NIAH identifies the house as part of a substantial terrace built in 1847 by Isaac Warren, steward of the Vernon estate, on land obtained from that estate. The terrace, its outbuildings, associated former gate lodge and shared green form a largely intact example of large-scale mid-nineteenth-century housing development along the Clontarf seafront. Historic fabric survives particularly at the entrance platform, door surround and railings.
access_status: NIAH records the building as a private house. Photograph from lawful public viewpoints only. Do not enter the property, shared green, rear outbuilding or private grounds. The NIAH describes replacement uPVC windows; record the current appearance accurately and do not infer original window details from the listing.
